pronunciation.approximation: HAIR-mohthr — the ó is long; the ð is the soft 'th' of 'this'; the final -r is the nominative ending, lightly sounded.
pronunciation.note: Old Norse Hermóðr is a transparent compound: herr ("host, army") + móðr ("spirit, mood, courage" — the same word as English "mood" and German "Mut"), whence the standard rendering "war-spirit." The restoration Hermóðr keeps the two things the ASCII form "Hermod" erases: the long ó and the letter ð (eth), the voiced dental fricative Old Norse wrote with its own character. Tier-1 by rule: two distinctive features preserved.

domains.title: The Rider of the Nine Nights
domains.subtitle: The Errand, the Bridge of Gold, and the Ransom of Baldr
domains.lead: Hermóðr is Óðinn's son and the boldest rider of the Æsir: the god who volunteered, when Baldr lay dead, to mount Sleipnir and ride nine nights through darkness to the halls of Hel, to ransom the light of the world back from the land of the dead.

cards.name: Sleipnir
cards.desc: Óðinn's eight-legged horse, lent for the descent — the only mount that can leap the gates of Hel.

cards.name: The Gjallarbrú
cards.desc: The bridge over the river Gjöll, thatched with glowing gold, where the maiden Móðguðr challenges the living.

cards.name: Draupnir
cards.desc: The drip-gold ring Óðinn laid on Baldr's pyre, sent back from Hel as proof the errand reached its mark.

cards.name: Helmet and Byrnie
cards.desc: The gifts of Óðinn named in Hyndluljóðr: war-gear for a son whose name means war-spirit.

symbols.name: Sleipnir's eight legs

symbols.name: The ring Draupnir
symbols.meaning: The token carried back from death as evidence and promise

symbols.name: The nine nights

mythology.lead: Hermóðr has essentially one story, and it is the noblest errand in the Edda: the ride to ransom Baldr, told in Gylfaginning with the plainness of a chronicle and the weight of a funeral.

myths.title: The Errand of the Nine Nights
myths.text: When Baldr fell to the mistletoe dart and the gods' grief had spent itself, Frigg asked who among the Æsir would ride the road to Hel and offer a ransom. Hermóðr the Bold, called Óðinn's sveinn — his lad, his attendant — stood up. They brought him Sleipnir, and he rode nine nights through valleys so dark and deep that he saw nothing until he reached the river Gjöll and the Gjallarbrú, the bridge roofed with glowing gold. There the maiden Móðguðr asked his name and lineage, and told him the bridge had thundered less under five companies of the dead the day before than under him alone.

myths.title: The Gate and the Hall
myths.text: He rode on to Helgrindr, the barred gate of the dead, tightened the stirrups, and spurred Sleipnir — and the horse leapt the gate with room to spare. In the hall he found his brother Baldr seated in the high seat, and he stayed the night. In the morning he begged Hel to let Baldr ride home with him, telling how great the weeping was among the Æsir. Hel's answer became the condition on which the whole ending turns: if all things in the world, living and dead, weep for Baldr, he may return; if anything refuses, Hel keeps him.

myths.title: The Ring and the Refusal
myths.text: Baldr sent back the ring Draupnir — the same ring Óðinn had laid on the pyre — and Nanna sent a linen headdress to Frigg and a gold ring to Fulla. Hermóðr carried the tokens and the tidings home, and the Æsir sent messengers through the world to ask all things to weep. All did — trees, stones, metals, beasts — save one giantess in a cave who called herself Þǫkk, Thanks, and wept dry tears: "let Hel hold what she has." The gods suspected it was Loki in disguise. Baldr stayed, and Hermóðr's nine nights stand in the Edda as the proof that even the boldest errand can be answered with a single refusal.

myths.title: The Gifts of the Father
myths.text: The Poetic Edda's Hyndluljóðr preserves the only other clear notice of him: among the gifts Óðinn dealt to his chosen, "he gave Hermóðr a helmet and a byrnie, and Sigmundr a sword." War-gear from the Allfather fits the name — herr, the host, and móðr, the war-spirit — and scholars have long noted the echo in Beowulf's Heremōd, the Danish king whose courage curdled into failure. The two figures share a name and little else: the Edda's Hermóðr keeps the name honorable.

lore.syncretism: The temptation to compare Hermóðr with Hermēs is as old as philology itself — the divine messenger riding between worlds looks like the Greek god's portrait. The comparison has been argued and abandoned for a century: the name is transparently Germanic (herr + móðr), not a borrowing, and the errand-rider is a role the North could grow on its own. What the comparison gets right is the shape of the job: where Hermēs is a psychopomp by office, Hermóðr becomes one for a single night, by courage. His cognate in the heroic record is Beowulf's Heremōd, and his kin in the pantheon are the other sons Óðinn spends on impossible errands — none of whom rode farther.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hermóðr left few traces outside the texts — no cult, no toponyms securely his — but the ride itself became one of the defining images of Norse myth: the nine nights, the golden bridge, the gate leapt in the dark. Modern retellings from Victorian mythographies to present-day novels and games cast him as the North's answer to Orpheus, the one who goes down to bargain with death and nearly wins. His name survives in the Icelandic given name Hermóður, and in scholarship as the standing example of the Edda's gift for making a minor god carry the grief of the whole world.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hermóðr is the patron of the necessary errand — the message someone has to carry, the door someone has to knock on, the descent someone has to volunteer for. He does everything right: the right horse, the right words, the right tokens. And still the answer is no. The Edda keeps him for that: proof that courage is owed regardless of the outcome, and that the errand, not the result, is what a name is made of.
lore.archaeology: Hermóðr is a textual figure: his attestations are the Codex Regius and its sister manuscripts of the Prose Edda (13th-14th c.) and the Hyndluljóðr preserved in the Flateyjarbók. No cult sites, toponyms, or inscriptions name him securely. The Gotland picture stones are his nearest material kin: the rider on the eight-legged horse on stones such as Ardre VIII is conventionally read as Óðinn or a hero on Sleipnir, and scholars have long wondered whether the image tradition knew the descent-ride that Gylfaginning tells.
